lesson.menu_desc: Answering requests with a conditional yes (as long as / provided that / unless), pushing back politely and a reading from an advice column -- reading model -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 34 — Saying Yes, with Conditions
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 34 — Saying Yes, with Conditions
lesson.grammar_point: conditional linkers for a conditional yes (as long as / provided that / unless + present)

listenings.text: Here is a small experiment. For one week, do not say a simple yes to any request. Add a condition instead. I can help, as long as we start after lunch. Yes, provided that you send me the details today. I will be there, unless my train is late. You will notice two things. First, almost nobody gets angry. People hear the yes first, and the condition feels fair. Second, your week becomes yours again. A condition is not a no. It is information. It tells the other person what you need to do a good job. And when you really can say yes without conditions, it feels like a gift.

Last year, my neighbor asked me to look after her dog for two weeks while she traveled. I love dogs, but I work from home and I have a lot of calls. So I said yes, as long as she could pay a dog walker for the mornings. She agreed. It worked perfectly. The dog was happy, my calls were quiet, and my neighbor was very grateful. This year she asked again, but for a whole month. I pushed back a little. I said, I can do two weeks, unless you find nobody else. In the end, we met halfway. Her sister took the dog for the first two weeks, and I took him for the last two.

extra_audio.text: First, I listen to the whole request. Then I check my week: am I already spread too thin? After that, I say yes, but with a condition: as long as it can wait until Monday. Next, if the other person pushes back, I try to meet them halfway. In the end, I ask for a heads-up next time.

reading.rtitle: Dear Clara: I can't say no
paras: Dear Clara, I have a problem with one small word: no. My colleagues ask me for favors every day. Can you cover for me on Friday? Can you take on this client? Can you check my presentation? I always say yes, and now I am spread too thin. I work late every night, and my own projects are behind. What should I do? -- Tired in Curitiba

Dear Tired, you do not need to say no. You need a better yes. Next time, try a yes with a condition. "Sure, I can check your presentation, as long as you send it before lunch." "Yes, I can take on the client, provided that someone else does the monthly report." The other person still hears a yes, and you keep control of your time.

It is also fine to push back on dates. "I can do it, but not this week, unless it is really urgent." Most people will meet you halfway. And ask for a heads-up: a request on Monday morning is easier than one on Friday at five.
Finally, choose your exceptions. If a friend in a real crisis needs you, make an exception and go out of your way. But if you say yes to everything, your yes stops meaning anything. -- Clara
